tier_reason: The record's 19.5x / 1.6x figures are misattributed: a WebSearch result ties them to a different Elafrou/Goumas/Koziris paper ('Performance Analysis and Optimization of Sparse Matrix-Vector Multiplication on Modern Multi- and Many-Core Processors', arXiv 1711.05487), whose CSR-based optimizer, not SparseX/CSX, beats MKL inspector-executor. The SparseX TOMS 2018 abstract, as quoted in search results, says only 'superior performance over competitive libraries on large-scale problems' and 'comparable performance to Intel MKL and ViennaCL'; the README, User's Guide (doc/SparseX_UG.pdf) and repo hold no numbers, so D.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No verified numbers. SparseX TOMS 2018 abstract (search-result quote): superior performance over competitive libraries on large-scale problems, comparable performance to Intel MKL and ViennaCL. The earlier '19.5x over MKL inspector-executor (1.6x average) for HPC matrices' belongs to a different paper by the same group (arXiv 1711.05487, a CSR-based optimizer), not to SparseX.
corrections.baseline: Intel MKL CSR SpMV (and pOSKI, ViennaCL in the TOMS paper)
corrections.caveats: No numbers for SparseX itself could be verified: the TOMS paper (dl.acm.org) and the SparseX home page are blocked here, and its abstract as quoted only claims superior performance on large-scale problems and comparable performance to MKL and ViennaCL. The figure the search agent recorded (up to 19.5x, 1.6x average over MKL inspector-executor for HPC matrices) comes from a different paper by the same authors (arXiv 1711.05487) about a CSR-based optimization selector, so it does not apply to SparseX. A 2025 third-party paper (DIV, ICS 2025; snippet only) says SparseX mainly speeds up SpMV for large matrices, median 13 percent, geometric mean 7.7 percent, baseline not visible. The repo ships a benchmark driver (src/bench, bench_spmv with --enable-bench and --with-mkl / pOSKI) but no results. Requires LLVM/Clang >= 4 for its JIT and notes every LLVM release breaks the JIT module; last commit 2018 (LLVM 6 support), so it likely does not build against current LLVM.

notes: Shortcoming to record: claimed speedup misattributed (numbers belong to arXiv 1711.05487, not SparseX). Kept as D rather than rejected because SparseX is a peer-reviewed TOMS library that later SpMV papers still benchmark against; under the keep-and-document rule it stays with this shortcoming. Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE.txt), 43 stars, 9 forks, 701 commits, last commit 2018-06-10 (abandoned).

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: spECK is a peer-reviewed PPoPP '20 paper (doi 10.1145/3332466.3374521, README bibtex), and a search result quoting its abstract says it outperforms all available GPU SpGEMM solutions in 79 percent of cases over matrices with more than 15k products, on average 83 percent faster than the second-best approach and up to 25x faster. B rests on venue plus abstract per earlier precedents; the paper (dl.acm.org, tugraz.at PDF) is blocked and the repo has a runner (runspECK with config.ini timing) but no results, CPU model or stated flags, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: PPoPP '20 abstract (search-result quote): outperforms all currently available GPU SpGEMM solutions in 79 percent of cases over all matrices with more than 15k products and is second best in 15 percent, on average 83 percent faster than the second-best approach and up to 25x faster. A later third-party study ('Optimizing General Sparse Matrix-Matrix Multiplication on the GPU', ACM, doi 10.1145/3774654) reportedly gives spECK 5.67x average over cuSPARSE (OpSparse 4.91x, TileSpGEMM 3.47x) (snippet only, not verified here).
corrections.workload: Sparse general matrix-matrix multiplication (SpGEMM) in CSR on NVIDIA GPUs over a large SuiteSparse-derived matrix set (PPoPP '20 evaluation; matrix count and GPU not seen), compared with other GPU SpGEMM libraries.
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from abstract quotes in search results; the PPoPP '20 paper (dl.acm.org, tugraz.at PDF) is blocked here, so GPU, CUDA version and the exact baseline list were not seen, and the quoted abstract does not single out cuSPARSE (the repo's harness checks results against cuSPARSE via externals/cusparse and config.ini CompareResult). Newer peer-reviewed work beats spECK: OpSparse (IEEE Access 2022) reports 1.52x average over spECK, and TileSpGEMM (PPoPP '22) is faster on 94 of 142 large matrices (spECK wins on 48). The 5.67x average over cuSPARSE comes from a third-party snippet the search agent saw and was not re-verified. Builds need per-GPU shared-memory constants set by hand in include/Multiply.h; CUDA 11+ needs the cuda11 branch. Last commit 2022-07-29, which fixed a readOperations kernel bug on matrices whose last row is empty.

notes: Metadata checked: MIT (LICENSE, 2019 Mathias Parger), 61 stars, 15 forks, 15 commits on master, last commit 2022-07-29 (abandoned). spECK is also vendored inside lorentzbf/OpSparse for comparison, which is not a duplicate issue for this entry.

corrections.caveats: Numbers come from the PPoPP '22 abstract as quoted in search results; the paper itself (dl.acm.org, ppopp22.sigplan.org) was not opened. This verifier's search confirmed the win counts (139, 138, 127 and 94 of 142 matrices executing at least one billion flops); the 'up to' maxima (2.78x, 145.35x, 97.86x, 3.70x) come from the search agent's snippet. Maxima are best cases; spECK is faster on 48 of 142 matrices, and the 145x/98x maxima are against bhSPARSE/NSPARSE, not cuSPARSE (2.78x maximum). A later third-party snippet puts TileSpGEMM's average at 3.47x over cuSPARSE, below spECK (5.67x) and OpSparse (4.91x). The repo's test program checks output against cuSPARSE and prints runtime and GFLOPS per matrix; README recommends a compute capability 8.6 GPU, but the GPU and host CPU used in the paper were not seen. No license file, so usability is 'reference'. Last commit 2022-11-09.
